claim: All-optical methods for imaging and manipulating brain networks with high spatial resolution are fundamental to study how neuronal ensembles drive behavior.
source: All-optical methods for imaging and manipulating brain networks with high spatial resolution are fundamental to study how neuronal ensembles drive behavior.
evidence: This is a statement of scientific consensus about the importance of all-optical methods in neuroscience research.

claim: Stimulation of neuronal ensembles using two-photon holographic techniques requires high-sensitivity actuators to avoid photodamage and heating.
source: Stimulation of neuronal ensembles using two-photon holographic techniques requires high-sensitivity actuators to avoid photodamage and heating.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about the requirements for safe two-photon optogenetic stimulation.

claim: Two-photon-excitable opsins should be insensitive to light at wavelengths used for imaging.
source: Moreover, two-photon-excitable opsins should be insensitive to light at wavelengths used for imaging.
evidence: This is a design requirement inferred from the need to minimize crosstalk between imaging and stimulation.

claim: A novel soma-targeted variant of the large-conductance blue-light-sensitive opsin CoChR (stCoChR) was developed.
source: To achieve this goal, we developed a novel soma-targeted variant of the large-conductance blue-light-sensitive opsin CoChR (stCoChR).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study describing the development of a new opsin variant.

claim: In the mouse cortex in vivo, holographic two-photon stimulation of stCoChR was combined with an amplified laser tuned at the opsin absorption peak and two-photon imaging of the red-shifted indicator jRCaMP1a.
source: In the mouse cortex in vivo, we combined holographic two-photon stimulation of stCoChR with an amplified laser tuned at the opsin absorption peak and two-photon imaging of the red-shifted indicator jRCaMP1a.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: Compared to previously characterized blue-light-sensitive soma-targeted opsins in vivo, stCoChR allowed neuronal stimulation with more than 10-fold lower average power.
source: Compared to previously characterized blue-light-sensitive soma-targeted opsins in vivo, stCoChR allowed neuronal stimulation with more than 10-fold lower average power and no spectral crosstalk.
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of stCoChR performance to previous opsins, supported by experimental data.

claim: stCoChR showed no spectral crosstalk compared to previously characterized blue-light-sensitive soma-targeted opsins in vivo.
source: Compared to previously characterized blue-light-sensitive soma-targeted opsins in vivo, stCoChR allowed neuronal stimulation with more than 10-fold lower average power and no spectral crosstalk.
evidence: This is a finding from the study comparing stCoChR to other opsins.

claim: The electrical activity of most brain circuits is organized in complex spatial and temporal patterns during information processing, storage, and retrieval.
source: During information processing, storage, and retrieval, the electrical activity of most brain circuits is organized in complex spatial and temporal patterns (Ni et al., 2018; Salinas and Sejnowski, 2001; Shahidi et al., 2019; Shamir and Sompolinsky, 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: The coding rules intrinsic to activity patterns are believed to underlie fundamental operating principles of brain networks.
source: The coding rules intrinsic to these activity patterns are believed to underlie fundamental operating principles of brain networks (Averbeck et al., 2006; Panzeri et al., 2017; Yuste, 2015).
evidence: This is a theoretical statement supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Recent techniques for all-optical interrogation of neural circuits allow for the first time to causally investigate coding rules with unprecedented spatial resolution in living mice.
source: Recent techniques for all-optical interrogation of neural circuits allow for the first time to causally investigate these coding rules with unprecedented spatial resolution in living mice (Carrillo-Reid et al., 2019; Chettih and Harvey, 2019; Gill et al., 2020; Marshel et al., 2019; ).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to recent studies demonstrating these capabilities.

claim: Two-photon calcium imaging combined with two-photon optogenetics makes it possible to simultaneously monitor and manipulate dozens of neurons with near single-cell resolution.
source: In particular, two-photon calcium imaging combined with two-photon optogenetics makes it possible to simultaneously monitor and manipulate dozens of neurons with near single-cell resolution (Bovetti and Fellin, 2015; Chen et al., 2019; Forli et al., 2018; Mardinly et al., 2018; Packer et al., 2015; Rickgauer et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work demonstrating these capabilities.

claim: The average power of illumination used to stimulate neurons is proportional to the probability of introducing thermal damage to brain tissue and unwanted modulation of neuronal physiology.
source: First, since the average power of illumination used to stimulate neurons is proportional to the probability of introducing thermal damage to brain tissue and unwanted modulation of neuronal physiology (Owen et al., 2019; Picot et al., 2018), maximizing the efficiency of optogenetic stimulation by increasing opsin excitation and photocurrent is of utmost importance.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to studies on photodamage and thermal effects.

claim: Maximizing the efficiency of optogenetic stimulation by increasing opsin excitation and photocurrent is of utmost importance.
source: First, since the average power of illumination used to stimulate neurons is proportional to the probability of introducing thermal damage to brain tissue and unwanted modulation of neuronal physiology (Owen et al., 2019; Picot et al., 2018), maximizing the efficiency of optogenetic stimulation by increasing opsin excitation and photocurrent is of utmost importance.
evidence: This is an inference based on the relationship between illumination power and tissue damage.

claim: There is a need for the development of novel high-efficiency, large-conductance opsins and efficient illumination strategies for their two-photon activation.
source: Thus, there is a need for the development of novel high-efficiency, large-conductance opsins and efficient illumination strategies for their two-photon activation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the identified challenges in the field.

claim: The crosstalk between imaging and stimulation needs to be minimized.
source: Second, the crosstalk between imaging and stimulation, that is, the unwanted activation of opsin-expressing neurons by imaging light, needs to be minimized (Forli et al., 2018; Packer et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a design requirement supported by citations to previous work identifying this issue.

claim: Crosstalk is due to the overlap between the two-photon absorption spectra of the opsin and of the calcium sensor.
source: This effect is due to the overlap between the two-photon absorption spectra of the opsin and of the calcium sensor (Venkatachalam and Cohen, 2014), and it is typically pronounced for red-shifted opsins, such as C1V1 (Yizhar et al., 2011) and ReaChR (Lin et al., 2013), which are used in combination with blue-light-sensitive indicators (e.g. GCaMP6 [Chen et al., 2013]).
evidence: This explanation is supported by a citation and examples from previous work.

claim: Crosstalk is typically pronounced for red-shifted opsins such as C1V1 and ReaChR, which are used in combination with blue-light-sensitive indicators.
source: This effect is due to the overlap between the two-photon absorption spectra of the opsin and of the calcium sensor (Venkatachalam and Cohen, 2014), and it is typically pronounced for red-shifted opsins, such as C1V1 (Yizhar et al., 2011) and ReaChR (Lin et al., 2013), which are used in combination with blue-light-sensitive indicators (e.g. GCaMP6 [Chen et al., 2013]).
evidence: This is supported by citations to specific opsins and indicators.

claim: Crosstalk may lead to non-negligible neuronal activation during two-photon imaging of the blue-light-sensitive indicator.
source: This process may lead to non-negligible neuronal activation during two-photon imaging of the blue-light-sensitive indicator (Packer et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work demonstrating this effect.

claim: Non-selective excitation of neurons in the field-of-view due to crosstalk could promote the formation of unwanted cell-assemblies.
source: The non-selective excitation of neurons in the field-of-view (FOV) due to this type of crosstalk could promote the formation of unwanted cell-assemblies (Carrillo-Reid et al., 2016) and bias the activity in the monitored area, complicating the interpretation of biological results (Emiliani et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a potential consequence supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The use of blue-shifted opsins combined with red-shifted calcium sensors was proved to be a valid approach, which largely eliminates the effect of the imaging beam on opsin excitation.
source: The use of blue-shifted opsins (e.g, ChR2 [Nagel et al., 2003] and GtACR2 [Govorunova et al., 2015]) combined with red-shifted calcium sensors (e.g. jRCaMP1a [Dana et al., 2016]) was proved to be a valid approach, which largely eliminates the effect of the imaging beam on opsin excitation while allowing simultaneous imaging and bidirectional manipulation of neural activity in vivo (Forli et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work demonstrating this approach.

claim: The limited photocurrent of ChR2 prevented the efficient stimulation of multiple neurons with low average power delivery to the brain tissue.
source: However, the limited photocurrent of ChR2 (Nagel et al., 2003) prevented the efficient stimulation of multiple neurons with low average power delivery to the brain tissue.
evidence: This is a limitation of ChR2 supported by a citation.

claim: stCoChR is derived from the large-conductance opsin CoChR.
source: To address this limitation, we describe here a new high-efficiency blue-light-sensitive opsin (stCoChR), derived from the large-conductance opsin CoChR (Klapoetke et al., 2014), which was targeted to the soma using the Kv2.1 targeting sequence (Lim et al., 2000).
evidence: This describes the origin and design of stCoChR, supported by citations.

claim: stCoChR was targeted to the soma using the Kv2.1 targeting sequence.
source: To address this limitation, we describe here a new high-efficiency blue-light-sensitive opsin (stCoChR), derived from the large-conductance opsin CoChR (Klapoetke et al., 2014), which was targeted to the soma using the Kv2.1 targeting sequence (Lim et al., 2000).
evidence: This describes the targeting strategy used for stCoChR, supported by a citation.

claim: stCoChR was combined with holographic two-photon stimulation, low repetition rate laser source excitation tuned at the peak of the opsin absorption spectrum, and imaging of the red-shifted functional indicator jRCaMP1a in vivo.
source: We combined stCoChR with holographic two-photon stimulation, low repetition rate laser source excitation tuned at the peak of the opsin absorption spectrum, and imaging of the red-shifted functional indicator jRCaMP1a (Dana et al., 2016) in vivo.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: Photocurrents elicited by stCoChR did not differ from those elicited by CoChR under two-photon scanning with a spiral pattern over the soma.
source: Upon two-photon (2P) scanning (λ = 940 nm) with a spiral pattern over the soma, photocurrents elicited by stCoChR did not differ from those elicited by CoChR, but were ~130-fold higher than those elicited by soCoChR under the same conditions (Figure 1A,B and Supplementary file 1- Supplementary Table 1; stCoChR: 1927.4 ± 283.3 pA, n = 10 cells; CoChR: 712.3 ± 188.9 pA, n = 11 cells; soCoChR: 14.9 ± 4.2 pA, n = 10 cells; Kruskal-Wallis test with post hoc comparisons: stCoChR vs CoChR, p=0.11; stCoChR vs soCoChR, p=3.8E–6).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from in vitro electrophysiology experiments, supported by statistical analysis and figure reference.

claim: Photocurrents elicited by stCoChR were ~130-fold higher than those elicited by soCoChR under two-photon scanning with a spiral pattern over the soma.
source: Upon two-photon (2P) scanning (λ = 940 nm) with a spiral pattern over the soma, photocurrents elicited by stCoChR did not differ from those elicited by CoChR, but were ~130-fold higher than those elicited by soCoChR under the same conditions (Figure 1A,B and Supplementary file 1- Supplementary Table 1; stCoChR: 1927.4 ± 283.3 pA, n = 10 cells; CoChR: 712.3 ± 188.9 pA, n = 11 cells; soCoChR: 14.9 ± 4.2 pA, n = 10 cells; Kruskal-Wallis test with post hoc comparisons: stCoChR vs CoChR, p=0.11; stCoChR vs soCoChR, p=3.8E–6).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from in vitro electrophysiology experiments, supported by statistical analysis and figure reference.

claim: Under one-photon full-field illumination, photocurrents elicited by stCoChR were similar to those of CoChR.
source: Under one-photon (1P) full-field illumination covering the soma and neurites (illumination area ~0.66 mm2), photocurrents elicited by stCoChR were similar to those of CoChR, but were approximately 40-fold higher than photocurrents elicited by soCoChR (Figure 1B and Supplementary file 1- Supplementary Table 2; stCoChR: 3709.5 ± 381.2 pA, n = 14 cells; CoChR: 3296.3 ± 452.4 pA, n = 14 cells; soCoChR: 91.8 ± 9.7 pA, n = 11 cells; Kruskal-Wallis test with post hoc comparisons: stCoChR vs CoChR, p=0.87; stCoChR vs soCoChR, p=2.2E–5).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from in vitro electrophysiology experiments, supported by statistical analysis and figure reference.

claim: Under one-photon full-field illumination, photocurrents elicited by stCoChR were approximately 40-fold higher than photocurrents elicited by soCoChR.
source: Under one-photon (1P) full-field illumination covering the soma and neurites (illumination area ~0.66 mm2), photocurrents elicited by stCoChR were similar to those of CoChR, but were approximately 40-fold higher than photocurrents elicited by soCoChR (Figure 1B and Supplementary file 1- Supplementary Table 2; stCoChR: 3709.5 ± 381.2 pA, n = 14 cells; CoChR: 3296.3 ± 452.4 pA, n = 14 cells; soCoChR: 91.8 ± 9.7 pA, n = 11 cells; Kruskal-Wallis test with post hoc comparisons: stCoChR vs CoChR, p=0.87; stCoChR vs soCoChR, p=2.2E–5).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from in vitro electrophysiology experiments, supported by statistical analysis and figure reference.

claim: The ratio between the photocurrents observed under 2P soma scanning and under 1P full-field illumination per cell was higher for stCoChR than both CoChR and soCoChR.
source: We found that this ratio was higher for stCoChR than both CoChR and soCoChR, whereas it did not differ between soCoChR and CoChR (stCoChR: 0.53 ± 0.06, n = 10 cells; CoChR: 0.18 ± 0.04, n = 11 cells; soCoChR: 0.15 ± 0.03, n = 10 cells; Kruskal-Wallis test with post hoc comparisons: stCoChR vs CoChR, p=8.4E-3; stCoChR vs soCoChR, p=1.3E-3; soCoChR vs CoChR, p=0.80), suggesting that the Kv2.1 motif in stCoChR concentrates the opsin molecules at the somatic region.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from in vitro electrophysiology experiments, supported by statistical analysis and figure reference.

claim: The Kv2.1 motif in stCoChR concentrates the opsin molecules at the somatic region.
source: We found that this ratio was higher for stCoChR than both CoChR and soCoChR, whereas it did not differ between soCoChR and CoChR (stCoChR: 0.53 ± 0.06, n = 10 cells; CoChR: 0.18 ± 0.04, n = 11 cells; soCoChR: 0.15 ± 0.03, n = 10 cells; Kruskal-Wallis test with post hoc comparisons: stCoChR vs CoChR, p=8.4E-3; stCoChR vs soCoChR, p=1.3E-3; soCoChR vs CoChR, p=0.80), suggesting that the Kv2.1 motif in stCoChR concentrates the opsin molecules at the somatic region.
evidence: This is an inference based on the photocurrent ratio data.

claim: The photocurrent in cells expressing stCoChR decayed at shorter distances when the stimulation spiral moved away from the soma along the path of the neurites compared with cells expressing CoChR.
source: We found that the photocurrent in cells expressing stCoChR decayed at shorter distances when the stimulation spiral moved away from the soma along the path of the neurites compared with cells expressing CoChR, whereas the decay length constant did not differ between stCoChR and soCoChR and between soCoChR and CoChR (Figure 1E and Supplementary file 1- Supplementary Table 4; stCoChR: τdecay = 16.1 ± 1.9 µm, n = 10 cells; CoChR: τdecay = 35.4 ± 6.6 µm, n = 11 cells; soCoChR: τdecay = 27.2 ± 6.2, n = 10 cells; Kruskal-Wallis test with post hoc comparisons: stCoChR vs CoChR, p=3.8E-2; stCoChR vs soCoChR, p=0.46; soCoChR vs CoChR, p=0.43).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from in vitro electrophysiology experiments, supported by statistical analysis and figure reference.

claim: stCoChR maintains the overall superior photocurrents characteristic of CoChR while a larger fraction of the current arises from opsin molecules in the somatic membrane.
source: These results suggest that stCoChR maintains the overall superior photocurrents characteristic of CoChR while a larger fraction of the current arises from opsin molecules in the somatic membrane.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the photocurrent and decay length data.

claim: There was a significant increase in the firing rate of stCoChR-expressing neurons during holographic two-photon stimulation in vivo.
source: We observed a significant increase in the firing rate of the recorded neuron during the stimulation period (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a finding from in vivo electrophysiology experiments, supported by figure reference.

claim: Neuronal responses to holographic two-photon stimulation increased with the average power of stimulation.
source: Neuronal responses to holographic two-photon stimulation increased with the average power of stimulation (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is a finding from in vivo electrophysiology experiments, supported by figure reference.

claim: The firing frequency increase during two-photon illumination was significantly larger for stCoChR-positive neurons than for stChR2-expressing cells previously recorded under similar experimental conditions.
source: Importantly, the firing frequency increase during two-photon illumination was significantly larger for stCoChR-positive neurons than for stChR2-expressing cells previously recorded (Forli et al., 2018) under similar experimental conditions (unpaired Student's t-test, p=3.5E-3, for 10 mW average power; Mann-Whitney test, p=4.6E-5, for 30 mW average power, λstim = 920 nm, Figure 2F).
evidence: This is a comparative finding from in vivo electrophysiology experiments, supported by statistical analysis, figure reference, and citation.

claim: At all tested average powers (10, 20, and 30 mW), one or more spikes could be recorded in a time window of ≤100 ms with high probability during holographic stimulation of stCoChR-expressing neurons.
source: To evaluate the temporal precision of stimulation, we computed the action potential (AP) probability as a function of illumination duration: at all tested average powers (10, 20, and 30 mW), one or more spikes could be recorded in a time window of ≤100 ms with high probability (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is a finding from in vivo electrophysiology experiments, supported by figure reference.

claim: The latency to first spike and the jitter depended on the illumination power during holographic stimulation of stCoChR-expressing neurons.
source: The latency to first spike and the jitter depended on the illumination power (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is a finding from in vivo electrophysiology experiments, supported by figure reference.

claim: The half-response distance for holographic stimulation of stCoChR-expressing neurons was 4.4 ± 3.8 μm in the radial direction.
source: The half-response distance was 4.4 ± 3.8 μm in the radial direction, 17.8 ± 4.4 μm in the axial up (dorsal) direction, and 23.8 ± 4.3 μm in the axial down (ventral) direction (n = 6 neurons from five mice).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from in vivo electrophysiology experiments measuring spatial resolution.

claim: The half-response distance for holographic stimulation of stCoChR-expressing neurons was 17.8 ± 4.4 μm in the axial up (dorsal) direction.
source: The half-response distance was 4.4 ± 3.8 μm in the radial direction, 17.8 ± 4.4 μm in the axial up (dorsal) direction, and 23.8 ± 4.3 μm in the axial down (ventral) direction (n = 6 neurons from five mice).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from in vivo electrophysiology experiments measuring spatial resolution.

claim: The half-response distance for holographic stimulation of stCoChR-expressing neurons was 23.8 ± 4.3 μm in the axial down (ventral) direction.
source: The half-response distance was 4.4 ± 3.8 μm in the radial direction, 17.8 ± 4.4 μm in the axial up (dorsal) direction, and 23.8 ± 4.3 μm in the axial down (ventral) direction (n = 6 neurons from five mice).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from in vivo electrophysiology experiments measuring spatial resolution.

claim: stCoChR allows higher efficiency two-photon holographic stimulation compared to previously characterized blue-light-sensitive opsins in vivo, while maintaining high spatial resolution.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that stCoChR allows higher efficiency two-photon holographic stimulation compared to previously characterized blue-light-sensitive opsins in vivo (Chen et al., 2019; Forli et al., 2018), while maintaining high spatial resolution.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the in vivo stimulation data, supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The extended illumination approach spreads the energy of the laser pulse across the cell body volume of the stimulated targets.
source: The extended illumination approach that we used to stimulate neurons spreads the energy of the laser pulse across the cell body volume of the stimulated targets.
evidence: This describes a property of the illumination method used.

claim: The extended illumination approach decreases the energy density and the risk for instantaneous non-linear photodamage during illumination, allowing higher energies per pulse to be used.
source: This naturally decreases the energy density and the risk for instantaneous non-linear photodamage during illumination, allowing higher energies per pulse to be used.
evidence: This is an inference based on the properties of the extended illumination approach.

claim: There was a significant increase in the neuronal response using low-repetition rate laser sources compared to using high-repetition rate laser sources for stimulation of stCoChR-expressing neurons.
source: We found a significant increase (Wilcoxon signed rank test, p=0.031, n = 6 cells from two mice) in the neuronal response using low-repetition rate laser sources compared to using high-repetition rate laser sources (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from in vivo electrophysiology experiments comparing different laser repetition rates, supported by statistical analysis and figure reference.

claim: At 1 MHz repetition rate, one or more spikes could be recorded in ≤30 ms with high probability using 3 mW and 5 mW average stimulation power.
source: Using 3 mW and 5 mW average stimulation power, one or more spikes could be recorded in ≤30 ms with high probability (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is a finding from in vivo electrophysiology experiments on SST interneurons, supported by figure reference.

claim: The repetition rate of the stimulation laser could be further decreased below 1 MHz, while maintaining high-efficiency opsin stimulation and lowering average stimulation power.
source: Considering the slow decay time of the opsin photocurrent (in the ms range), we reasoned that the repetition rate of the stimulation laser could be further decreased below 1 MHz, while maintaining high-efficiency opsin stimulation and lowering average stimulation power.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the known properties of opsin photocurrents.

claim: AP probability non-linearly decreased with the repetition rate when stimulating stCoChR-expressing L2/3 principal cells at constant energy per pulse.
source: As shown in Figure 4C, we found that AP probability non-linearly decreased with the repetition rate.
evidence: This is a finding from in vivo electrophysiology experiments varying laser repetition rate, supported by figure reference.

claim: A similar AP probability during illumination was observed when stimulating at 1 MHz repetition rate with 1 mW average power and 1 nJ energy per pulse and when stimulating at 50 kHz repetition rate with 0.25 mW average power and 5 nJ energy per pulse.
source: A similar AP probability during illumination was observed when stimulating at 1 MHz repetition rate with 1 mW average power and lower energy per pulse (1 nJ) and when stimulating at 50 kHz repetition rate with 0.25 mW average power and higher energy per pulse (5 nJ) (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a finding from in vivo electrophysiology experiments comparing different stimulation parameters, supported by figure reference.

claim: stCoChR allows highly efficient two-photon holographic stimulation with low average power per cell (0.25–5 mW, depending on the laser repetition rate) and energy densities well below photodamage thresholds.
source: These results demonstrate highly efficient two-photon holographic stimulation of stCoChR with low average power per cell (0.25–5 mW, depending on the laser repetition rate) and energy densities well below photodamage thresholds (Charan et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the stimulation data, supported by citations to photodamage threshold studies.

claim: Raster scanning at 1100 nm did not significantly affect the firing activity of L2/3 neurons expressing stCoChR in vivo.
source: We found that raster scanning under these conditions did not significantly affect the firing activity of L2/3 neurons expressing stCoChR (Figure 5C, left).
evidence: This is a finding from in vivo electrophysiology experiments measuring crosstalk, supported by figure reference.

claim: Raster scanning at 920 nm and moderate power (30 mW) significantly increased the spiking activity of stCoChR-expressing neurons.
source: As an important control, we tuned the imaging laser to 920 nm (the wavelength used for holographic stimulation) and we found that raster scanning the same FOV at 920 nm and moderate power (laser power: 30 mW) significantly increased the spiking activity of stCoChR-expressing neurons (Figure 5B and C, right).
evidence: This is a finding from in vivo electrophysiology experiments measuring crosstalk, supported by figure reference.

claim: In neurons co-expressing stCoChR and jRCaMP1a, raster scanning at 1100 nm (imaging power: 30–35 mW) did not alter the spontaneous firing rate of imaged neurons.
source: Similarly to what we observed in cells expressing only stCoChR, we found that raster scanning at 1100 nm (imaging power: 30–35 mW) did not alter the spontaneous firing rate of imaged neurons (Figure 5E–F).
evidence: This is a finding from in vivo electrophysiology experiments measuring crosstalk in co-expressing neurons, supported by figure reference.

claim: In neurons co-expressing stCoChR and jRCaMP1a, raster scanning at 920 nm caused a large and significant increase in the neuron's spontaneous firing rate.
source: Moreover, raster scanning at 920 nm caused a large and significant increase in the neuron's spontaneous firing rate (Figure 5E–F).
evidence: This is a finding from in vivo electrophysiology experiments measuring crosstalk in co-expressing neurons, supported by figure reference.

claim: The average imaging power used to estimate the crosstalk (between 30 mW and 35 mW) was sufficient to detect jRCaMP1a fluorescence transients associated with spontaneous firing of APs.
source: Importantly, we verified that the average imaging power used to estimate the crosstalk (between 30 mW and 35 mW) was sufficient to detect jRCaMP1a fluorescence transients associated with spontaneous firing of APs (Figure 5G), similarly to previous reports (Dana et al., 2016; Forli et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a verification finding from in vivo imaging experiments, supported by figure reference and citations.

claim: In SST-positive interneurons expressing stCoChR, scanning at 1100 nm did not significantly raise the firing rate of recorded cells.
source: In agreement with our findings on principal cells, scanning stCoChR-positive interneurons at 1100 nm did not significantly raise the firing rate of recorded cells, while scanning at 920 nm did (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a finding from in vivo electrophysiology experiments on interneurons measuring crosstalk, supported by figure reference.

claim: In SST-positive interneurons expressing stCoChR, scanning at 920 nm significantly raised the firing rate of recorded cells.
source: In agreement with our findings on principal cells, scanning stCoChR-positive interneurons at 1100 nm did not significantly raise the firing rate of recorded cells, while scanning at 920 nm did (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a finding from in vivo electrophysiology experiments on interneurons measuring crosstalk, supported by figure reference.

claim: Imaging at longer wavelengths (~1100 nm) with average power allowing detection of calcium events (30–35 mW) does not significantly perturb the supra-threshold activity of stCoChR-positive principal neurons and interneurons.
source: Overall, these results demonstrate that imaging at longer wavelengths (~1100 nm) with average power allowing detection of calcium events (30–35 mW) does not significantly perturb the supra-threshold activity of stCoChR-positive principal neurons and interneurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the crosstalk experiments across different cell types.

claim: Consecutive holographic stimulation of stCoChR-expressing neurons typically evoked reliable fluorescence transients in the targeted cells.
source: We observed that consecutive holographic stimulation of stCoChR-expressing neurons typically evoked reliable fluorescence transients in the targeted cells (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a finding from all-optical experiments combining imaging and stimulation, supported by figure reference.

claim: Fluorescence transients in the stimulated cell could be evoked with low power (0.7 mW per cell at 0.1 MHz repetition rate).
source: We found that fluorescence transients in the stimulated cell could be evoked with low power (0.7 mW per cell at 0.1 MHz repetition rate, Figure 6D) and that increasing the repetition rate non-linearly increased the amplitude of the evoked fluorescence transients (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is a finding from all-optical experiments, supported by figure reference.

claim: Increasing the repetition rate non-linearly increased the amplitude of the evoked fluorescence transients.
source: We found that fluorescence transients in the stimulated cell could be evoked with low power (0.7 mW per cell at 0.1 MHz repetition rate, Figure 6D) and that increasing the repetition rate non-linearly increased the amplitude of the evoked fluorescence transients (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is a finding from all-optical experiments, supported by figure reference.

claim: jRCaMP1a transients induced by the photostimulation protocol were associated with the firing of 6.7 ± 1.9 APs (range 3–14).
source: We observed that jRCaMP1a transients induced by the used photostimulation protocol were associated with the firing of 6.7 ± 1.9 APs (range 3–14, n = 5 cells from three mice), in agreement with what we observed in cells expressing only stCoChR (Figure 2C–E).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from combined imaging and electrophysiology experiments, supported by figure reference.

claim: In cells expressing only jRCaMP1a, the photostimulation protocol did not increase AP frequency.
source: Importantly, in cells expressing only jRCaMP1a the same stimulation protocol did not increase AP frequency (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a control finding from electrophysiology experiments, supported by figure reference.

claim: stCoChR is a highly efficient blue-shifted opsin that can be used in combination with red-shifted calcium indicators to perform all-optical circuit interrogations with low average power delivery per cell and minimal crosstalk between imaging and photostimulation.
source: Altogether, these results demonstrate stCoChR is a highly efficient blue-shifted opsin that can be used in combination with red-shifted calcium indicators to perform all-optical circuit interrogations with low average power delivery per cell and minimal crosstalk between imaging and photostimulation.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the experimental findings in the study.

claim: The large-conductance blue-light-sensitive soma-targeted opsin, stCoChR, in combination with high-energy ultrafast laser sources tuned at the opsin's peak absorption wavelength, requires more than one order of magnitude lower average power per cell compared to previously characterized blue-light-sensitive soma-targeted opsins in vivo.

claim: Imaging conditions commonly used to monitor red-shifted functional indicators do not result in significant suprathreshold activation of stCoChR-expressing neurons.

claim: Red-shifted opsins are generally prone to unwanted activation during imaging of blue-light-sensitive indicators because of the intrinsic absorption properties of the retinal group at shorter wavelengths.

evidence: This is an explanation based on known properties of opsins, supported by citations.

claim: Combining blue-light-sensitive opsins (e.g. ChR2, GtACR2) with red-shifted indicators (jRCaMP1a) is a valid choice to effectively reduce crosstalk.
source: Previous work demonstrated that combining blue-light-sensitive opsins (e.g. ChR2, GtACR2) with red-shifted indicators (jRCaMP1a) is a valid choice to effectively reduce this form of crosstalk (Forli et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a finding from previous work, supported by citation.

claim: Despite the fact that stCoChR has a much larger photocurrent compared to ChR2, suprathreshold activation of stCoChR-expressing neurons during imaging at red-shifted wavelengths is not significant at imaging power <35 mW.
source: Importantly, despite the fact that stCoChR has a much larger photocurrent compared to ChR2 (Klapoetke et al., 2014), we show here that suprathreshold activation of stCoChR-expressing neurons during imaging at red-shifted wavelengths is not significant at imaging power <35 mW (Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the crosstalk experiments, supported by figure references and citation.

claim: Efficient two-photon excitation of blue-shifted opsins has largely been constrained by the limited availability of high-energy pulsed systems tuned at ~920 nm.

claim: Stimulation at 920 nm reduces tissue heating that is, in contrast, higher at the longer wavelengths (>1000 nm) commonly used to excite red-shifted opsins.

evidence: This is a finding from previous work, supported by citations.

claim: Lowering the laser repetition rate is advantageous for two-photon excitation of the retinal group.

source: Besides decreasing crosstalk, the choice of red-shifted indicators may facilitate imaging in deeper regions by using longer wavelengths, which are less sensitive to scattering (Helmchen and Denk, 2005).

claim: Holographic stimulation at 920 nm may decrease tissue heating which is higher at the longer wavelengths (λ = 1040 nm) used to stimulate red-shifted opsins.

evidence: This is an advantage of the approach used in the study, supported by citations.

claim: The extended illumination approach distributes the laser pulse energy across a much larger volume compared to scanning methods with diffraction-limited-spots.
source: Compared to scanning methods with diffraction-limited-spots (Carrillo-Reid et al., 2016; Carrillo-Reid et al., 2019; Chettih and Harvey, 2019; Marshel et al., 2019; Packer et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2018), our extended illumination approach distributes the laser pulse energy across a much larger volume, that is the cell body volume of the stimulated neuron.
evidence: This is a comparison of the approach used in the study to other methods, supported by citations.

claim: The instantaneous energy density and the consequent risk of non-linear photodamage are decreased with the extended illumination approach, allowing higher energy per pulse to be used.
source: Thus, the instantaneous energy density and the consequent risk of non-linear photodamage are decreased, allowing higher energy per pulse to be used.

source: Importantly, we found that, at 50 kHz repetition rate, stimulation of target cells could be achieved with <1 mW, more than one order of magnitude lower average power per cell compared to previously published blue-light-sensitive soma-targeted (st) opsins in vivo (Forli et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding comparing stCoChR to previous opsins, supported by citation.

claim: Two-photon holographic stimulation can be applied to cell types with different biophysical properties (principal cells and interneurons) with similar efficacy.
source: Importantly, we validated these findings across both principal cells and interneurons (SST+), showing that two-photon holographic stimulation can be applied to cell types with different biophysical properties with similar efficacy.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experiments in different cell types.

claim: The use of stCoChR in vivo, compared with other opsins including ST-ChroME, Chronos and the non-soma-targeted version of CoChR, allows photoexcitation with lower average power of excitation (1–5 mW at 1 MHz repetition rate, and potentially less at repetition rates < 1 MHz).
source: Altogether, the use of stCoChR in vivo, compared with other opsins including ST-ChroME, Chronos and the non-soma-targeted version of CoChR (Chen et al., 2019; Mardinly et al., 2018), allows photoexcitation with lower average power of excitation (1–5 mW at 1 MHz repetition rate, and potentially less at repetition rates < 1 MHz, Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a comparative conclusion based on the study's findings, supported by citations and figure references.

claim: The combination of stCoChR with tuned amplified laser stimulation and red-shifted functional indicators represents a powerful alternative approach to performing high-efficiency all-optical causal investigation of neural circuits in the intact brain with minimal crosstalk between the imaging and photostimulation channels.
source: The combination of stCoChR with tuned amplified laser stimulation and red-shifted functional indicators represents a powerful alternative approach to performing high-efficiency all-optical causal investigation of neural circuits in the intact brain with minimal crosstalk between the imaging and photostimulation channels.
